subChunks.title: Advanced Data Analysis & Scientific Visualisation
subChunks.hookHtml:
'John Snow did not have a computer,' Theodora said, placing a reproduction of the 1854 Broad Street cholera map on the table. 'He had a quill pen, a surveyor's notebook, and the insight to plot deaths as dots on a street map. The cluster around the Broad Street water pump leapt off the page. He persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump handle, and the outbreak ended. One visualisation. Thousands of lives.'

'Data visualisation is not decoration. It is a cognitive tool — a way of exploiting the human visual system, which devotes a third of the cerebral cortex to processing spatial patterns, to perform pattern recognition that pure numerics would take much longer to reveal. The statistician Francis Anscombe demonstrated this in 1973 with his famous quartet: four datasets with identical means, variances, and correlations that look completely different when plotted. If you only compute summary statistics, you are blind.'

She tapped the cholera map. 'The danger runs the other way too. Visualisation can mislead as readily as it illuminates — through cherry-picked axes, truncated scales, misrepresented uncertainty, and confusing causation with correlation in a beautifully rendered scatter plot. Analysing data well is a scientific skill with ethical weight. Decisions about drugs, policies, and investments hang on the figures scientists produce.'
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Exploratory Data Analysis

Exploratory data analysis (EDA), systematised by John Tukey (1977), is the initial phase of data analysis in which the analyst examines the data structure, identifies distributions, outliers, missing values, and patterns, without imposing a prior model. Tools: histograms (distribution shape), box plots (quartiles, outliers), scatter plots (bivariate relationships), correlation matrices, pair plots. EDA is not optional — it routinely reveals data quality issues, entry errors, unexpected distributions, and non-linear relationships that would invalidate downstream modelling.

Anscombe's quartet (1973): four datasets with identical summary statistics (mean x̄=9, ȳ=7.5, Var(x)=11, Var(y)≈4.12, r=0.816) that look entirely different when plotted — linear, curved, linear with an outlier, and a point cluster. A powerful warning that summary statistics without visualisation are insufficient.

Distributions and Transformations

Real data frequently violate the normality assumption required by many parametric tests. Diagnostic tools: Q-Q plots (quantile-quantile plots compare observed quantiles to theoretical normal quantiles — deviations indicate non-normality), Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests (formal normality tests, but sensitive to large samples). Transformations (log, square root, Box-Cox) can normalise right-skewed data. Heavy-tailed distributions (power laws, Student's t with few degrees of freedom) are common in natural science data and require appropriate methods.

Regression Analysis

Linear regression y = β₀ + β₁x + ε assumes: linearity, independence of errors, homoscedasticity (constant variance), and normality of residuals. Residual plots diagnose violations. Multiple regression extends to multiple predictors; multicollinearity (correlated predictors) inflates standard errors and destabilises coefficient estimates, detectable via the variance inflation factor (VIF > 5–10 is concerning).

Generalised linear models (GLMs) extend regression to non-normal responses: logistic regression for binary outcomes (logit link), Poisson regression for count data (log link). Model selection: AIC = 2k − 2ln(L̂) (Akaike Information Criterion, penalises model complexity); BIC = k ln(n) − 2ln(L̂) (stronger complexity penalty). Lower AIC/BIC indicates a better model. Cross-validation provides an empirical alternative to information criteria for predictive performance assessment.

Bayesian Analysis

Bayesian regression replaces point estimates with posterior distributions over parameters, incorporating prior knowledge and propagating uncertainty fully. Posterior predictive distributions quantify uncertainty in predictions, not just in parameters. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples the posterior when it cannot be computed analytically. Modern probabilistic programming languages (Stan, PyMC) make Bayesian modelling accessible. Bayesian approaches naturally handle small sample sizes and provide credible intervals (P(θ ∈ CI | data) = 95%) rather than frequentist confidence intervals (which do not have this interpretation).

Handling High-Dimensional Data

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projects high-dimensional data onto orthogonal principal components that capture maximum variance. The first k components form a low-dimensional subspace explaining Σ(λᵢ)/Σ(λ_total) × 100% of total variance. Used for exploratory analysis, noise reduction, and feature engineering. Limitations: linear method; sensitive to scaling (data must be standardised); principal components are not always interpretable.

t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding) and UMAP are nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods that preserve local structure, useful for visualising clusters in single-cell RNA-seq, image embeddings, and molecular fingerprints. They are not appropriate for quantitative distance measurement — only relative cluster structure.

Regularisation in regression prevents overfitting in high-dimensional settings where p ≫ n. Ridge regression (L2 penalty: λΣβᵢ²) shrinks coefficients toward zero without eliminating them. LASSO (L1 penalty: λΣ|βᵢ|) produces sparse solutions by setting some coefficients exactly to zero, performing implicit feature selection. The elastic net combines L1 and L2.

Multiple Testing and False Discovery

When testing many hypotheses simultaneously (genomics: 20,000 genes; neuroimaging: ~100,000 voxels), the probability of at least one false positive grows rapidly. With m tests at α = 0.05: expected false positives = 0.05m. The Bonferroni correction sets α' = α/m (conservative; reduces power). The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controls the false discovery rate (FDR): the expected proportion of false positives among all significant results. For genomics, FDR ≤ 0.05 means at most 5% of reported associations are false — more permissive than Bonferroni but appropriate for discovery-phase studies.

The winner's curse: the first study to find a significant result typically overestimates effect size due to publication bias and sampling variability. Pre-registration (registering hypothesis, sample size, and analysis plan before collecting data) mitigates this and distinguishes exploratory from confirmatory analysis.

Scientific Visualisation Principles

Effective scientific figures follow principles from cognitive science and information theory. Tufte's data-ink ratio: maximise the proportion of ink used to convey data; remove chart junk (3D effects, excessive gridlines, redundant labels). Cleveland's hierarchy: position on a common scale is more accurately perceived than length, then angle, then area, then colour. Prefer bar charts over pie charts; prefer scatter plots over bubble charts when precision matters.

Colour selection: use perceptually uniform colormaps (viridis, plasma) for sequential data — not the misleading rainbow. Use diverging colormaps (RdBu, coolwarm) for data centred on zero. Account for colour blindness (~8% of males): avoid red-green contrasts without additional encoding (shape, pattern, label). Error bars must specify what they represent — SD, SEM, 95% CI, range — as these are not interchangeable. Always report n and the error bar type.

storyBeats.text: 'Anscombe's quartet should be the first thing taught in every statistics course and the last thing forgotten,' Theodora said. 'Four datasets. Identical means, variances, correlations. One linear, one parabolic, one with an influential outlier, one a point cluster. Only plotting revealed the truth. Only plotting.'

'Residual plots are your diagnostic. After any regression, plot the residuals against fitted values. Any pattern — a funnel, a curve, a cluster — tells you the model assumptions are violated. Homoscedasticity, linearity, independence: the plot will catch problems the p-value hides.'

'Multiple testing is where careers end and papers get retracted. Test 20,000 genes at p < 0.05 and by chance alone you expect 1,000 false positives. Bonferroni corrects — but kills statistical power. Benjamini-Hochberg is the practical compromise: control the false discovery rate, not each individual error.'

'The winner's curse is subtle and insidious. The first study to find an effect overestimates it — selection bias ensures the estimate that crossed the significance threshold is inflated. Replication finds a smaller effect, and everyone calls it a failure of replication. Pre-registration is the only clean fix.'

'The rainbow colormap is banned in my group,' Theodora said firmly. 'It is perceptually non-uniform — a given data difference maps to different perceived colour differences in different parts of the range. Viridis is monotone in both colour and luminance. It degrades gracefully to greyscale and to colour-blind vision. Use it.'

'Error bars without labels are lies by omission. Standard deviation, standard error, 95% confidence interval — these are entirely different quantities. A narrow SEM bar on a small sample looks precise. It is not. Always label what your error bars show.'

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what Anscombe's quartet is and what lesson it teaches about the relationship between summary statistics and data visualisation.
learningObjectives: Apply EDA methods including Q-Q plots, residual analysis, and correlation matrices to assess data quality and distributional assumptions
Select appropriate regression models (linear, GLM, Bayesian) and model selection criteria (AIC/BIC) for a given research scenario
Apply Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections to multiple testing scenarios and explain the distinction between FWER and FDR control
Design effective scientific visualisations following cognitive principles and evaluate common visualisation pitfalls in published figures
commonMistakes: Interpreting 95% confidence intervals as 'there is a 95% probability the true parameter is in this range' — the correct interpretation is that 95% of such intervals constructed from repeated samples would contain the true value
Using standard error (SEM) as a measure of variability rather than of estimation precision — SEM decreases with sample size even when the population variability is unchanged
Applying Bonferroni correction to all multiple testing scenarios when FDR control (Benjamini-Hochberg) would be more appropriate for discovery-phase research
Using rainbow/jet colourmaps which are perceptually non-uniform and mislead quantitative data interpretation
assessmentCriteria: Correctly diagnoses regression assumption violations from residual plots and proposes appropriate remedies
Applies Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg correction to a multiple testing scenario and justifies the choice
Accurately interprets PCA output — proportion of variance explained, biplot interpretation — without over-interpreting component direction
Critiques a published scientific figure for colour choice, error bar labelling, and data-ink ratio, proposing specific improvements
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Regression Diagnostics and Multiple Testing

Part A: A neuroscientist fits a linear regression predicting reaction time (y, ms) from age (x₁, years) and caffeine intake (x₂, mg/day) across n = 60 participants. The residual plot shows a clear funnel shape — residuals increasing in spread with fitted values. What assumption is violated? What transformation might address it? How would this affect the interpretation of regression coefficients?

Part B: In a genome-wide association study (GWAS), 500,000 SNPs are tested for association with blood pressure at α = 0.05. How many false positives would be expected by chance? Calculate the Bonferroni-corrected threshold. If the study has 80% power to detect a true association at this corrected threshold, and there are 20 truly associated SNPs, how many would be detected?

Part C: A colleague presents a bar chart with error bars but no label specifying SD, SEM, or 95% CI. The sample size is n = 5 per group. Why does this matter particularly at small sample sizes? What information is missing and how would you request it?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Part A: The funnel-shaped residual plot indicates heteroscedasticity — non-constant variance of residuals across fitted values. This violates the homoscedasticity assumption of standard linear regression. Consequences: OLS estimates remain unbiased but are no longer minimum variance (BLUE); standard errors are incorrect, invalidating p-values and confidence intervals. Remedies: (1) Log-transform the outcome (log reaction time), often effective for right-skewed continuous outcomes; (2) Use weighted least squares (WLS) if variance can be modelled; (3) Use heteroscedasticity-robust (sandwich) standard errors. After transformation, regression coefficients interpret as multiplicative effects on reaction time rather than additive.

Part B: Expected false positives = 500,000 × 0.05 = 25,000 by chance. Bonferroni threshold: α' = 0.05/500,000 = 10⁻⁷. This is the standard GWAS threshold (often reported as p < 5×10⁻⁸ for additional caution). At 80% power for 20 true associations: expected detected = 20 × 0.80 = 16 true positives. Expected false positives at Bonferroni threshold: 500,000 × 10⁻⁷ = 0.05 — essentially zero. So approximately 16 true positives and ~0 false positives; total significant results ≈ 16.

Part C: At n = 5, SEM = SD/√5 ≈ 0.45 × SD. An SEM bar is roughly half the width of an SD bar, giving a misleading impression of precision. A 95% CI = mean ± t(0.025, df=4) × SEM ≈ mean ± 2.78 × SEM ≈ mean ± 1.24 × SD — wider than SEM, appropriately conveying uncertainty. For inference, 95% CI is most informative; for describing variability in the population, SD is most informative. Without the label, the bar is uninterpretable. You would request: (1) which measure the error bar represents, (2) confirmation of n per group, and (3) whether bars represent ±1 or ±2 of the measure.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A meta-analysis of 30 published studies on a psychological intervention finds a pooled effect size of d = 0.45 (95% CI: 0.28–0.62). A funnel plot shows marked asymmetry — small studies cluster to the right of the pooled estimate. Write a structured critique (~300 words) addressing: (a) what funnel plot asymmetry suggests about publication bias and how it affects interpretation of the pooled estimate; (b) what methods exist to correct for publication bias (trim-and-fill, Egger's test, p-curve analysis) and their assumptions; and (c) what recommendations you would make for future research in this area to reduce the risk of a biased evidence base.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) Funnel plot asymmetry: In an unbiased literature, a funnel plot (effect size vs. precision/sample size) should be symmetrical — small studies scatter widely around the pooled estimate (lower precision), large studies cluster tightly. Asymmetry with small studies reporting larger effects suggests publication bias: small studies with small or null effects are less likely to be published. The pooled estimate of d = 0.45 is therefore likely inflated — it overweights the published positive small-study literature and ignores the null results in file drawers. The true effect is probably smaller, possibly much smaller.

(b) Correction methods: Trim-and-fill adds hypothetical unpublished studies mirroring the asymmetric excess, then recomputes the pooled estimate. Assumption: the publication bias is symmetric around the true effect. Egger's test is a formal regression test for funnel asymmetry (y-intercept ≠ 0). It has low power in meta-analyses with few studies. P-curve analysis examines the distribution of reported p-values: genuine effects produce a right-skewed p-curve (many p-values near 0.05 is suspicious — suggests p-hacking). Selection models (Vevea-Hedges) explicitly model the probability of publication as a function of significance. All methods have assumptions and limitations; none definitively recovers the true effect. Bayesian hierarchical models incorporating publication probability are increasingly recommended.

(c) Recommendations: (1) Pre-register all future trials (registration on ClinicalTrials.gov or OSF) — mandatory reporting of null results regardless of outcome. (2) Use registered reports (journals commit to publish based on the merit of the question and design before data collection). (3) Conduct adequately powered confirmatory replications of the most promising pilot studies. (4) Pool individual patient data (IPD meta-analysis) rather than aggregate statistics — reduces reliance on published papers. (5) Adopt open data standards so unpublished datasets can be included in future meta-analyses. The goal is a symmetric funnel plot earned through transparent reporting, not statistical correction of a biased base.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Four datasets with identical summary statistics (mean, variance, correlation) that look completely different when plotted, demonstrating that visualisation is indispensable to data analysis.
A multiple testing correction that controls the false discovery rate (expected proportion of false positives among significant results) rather than the familywise error rate.
A measure of multicollinearity in multiple regression: VIF > 5–10 indicates that a predictor is strongly correlated with others, inflating its standard error and destabilising coefficient estimates.
Nonlinear dimensionality reduction algorithms that preserve local neighbourhood structure, widely used for visualising high-dimensional biological data such as single-cell transcriptomics.
Specifying a study's hypothesis, sample size, and analysis plan before data collection, distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory analysis and reducing p-hacking and publication bias.

questions.questionHtml: What does the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure control in a multiple testing scenario?
options: The false discovery rate (FDR) — the expected proportion of false positives among significant results
The familywise error rate (FWER) — the probability of any false positive across all tests
The Type II error rate — the probability of missing a true positive
The effect size inflation due to multiple comparison adjustments
questions.correctAnswer: The false discovery rate (FDR) — the expected proportion of false positives among significant results
questions.explanationHtml: Benjamini-Hochberg controls the FDR: if 100 hypotheses are tested and 20 are significant, with FDR = 0.05, at most 1 (5% of 20) is expected to be a false positive. This is less conservative than Bonferroni (which controls FWER — probability of any false positive) and is preferred in discovery-phase research like genomics where some false positives are acceptable to preserve statistical power.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher runs a multiple regression with three predictors. The VIF for one predictor is 12.4. What does this indicate and what should the researcher do?
options: Severe multicollinearity — this predictor is highly correlated with others; consider removing it, combining correlated predictors, or using ridge regression
A significant predictor — VIF > 10 indicates a large effect size
Heteroscedasticity — the variance of this predictor is not constant
The predictor is non-normally distributed and needs transformation before inclusion
questions.correctAnswer: Severe multicollinearity — this predictor is highly correlated with others; consider removing it, combining correlated predictors, or using ridge regression
questions.explanationHtml: VIF (variance inflation factor) measures how much the variance of a coefficient is inflated due to correlation with other predictors. VIF = 1/(1−R²_j) where R²_j is the R² from regressing predictor j on all other predictors. VIF > 5–10 is problematic: standard errors are inflated, making significance tests unreliable and coefficient estimates unstable. Remedies include removing the collinear predictor, combining correlated predictors (e.g., via PCA), or using regularisation (ridge/LASSO).

questions.questionHtml: A 95% confidence interval for a drug effect is [0.12, 0.48]. Which of the following interpretations is statistically correct?
options: If this experiment were repeated many times, 95% of such computed intervals would contain the true parameter value
There is a 95% probability that the true parameter falls between 0.12 and 0.48
We are 95% confident that the drug effect is positive, with 5% chance it is zero or negative
The drug effect is significant at p < 0.05 because zero is not in the interval, and the true effect is most likely near 0.30
questions.correctAnswer: If this experiment were repeated many times, 95% of such computed intervals would contain the true parameter value
questions.explanationHtml: The frequentist confidence interval is a statement about the procedure, not about the specific interval: 95% of intervals constructed using this procedure from repeated samples would contain the true (fixed) parameter. The specific observed interval either contains the true value or it does not — we cannot assign a probability to this. Option B is the Bayesian credible interval interpretation (valid in Bayesian analysis but not for frequentist CIs). Options C and D are common misconceptions; it is correct that p < 0.05 (since 0 is excluded) but the final clause about 'most likely near 0.30' is not a frequentist statement.
